tagline.text: A remnant urban forest on the Pasig River in Manila, known as "the lungs of Manila"

location.label: Location
location.text: Antonio Villegas Street (formerly Arroceros Street), Ermita, Manila, on the south bank of the Pasig River below Quezon Bridge

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (early morning or late afternoon recommended)

children.text: Arroceros Forest Park is an urban forest of about 2.2 hectares on the south bank of the Pasig River in Ermita, Manila. With old shade trees, birdsong and a riverside path, it is a good place to rest during a day of city sightseeing.

Arroceros Forest Park is an urban forest at the end of Antonio Villegas Street (formerly Arroceros Street) in Ermita, on the south bank of the Pasig River. It sits at the foot of Quezon Bridge and is presented as the only nature park run by the Manila city government. Figures for its size vary by source, but news reports most often give about 2.2 hectares. In the middle of Manila, packed with concrete buildings and traffic, the mere fact that a forest of this size survives is a highlight in itself, which is why locals call it "the last lung of Manila."

Its history goes back to the Spanish era. As the old name Arroceros ("rice sellers") suggests, the area was a rice market district and was later said to have housed a tobacco factory. In the American period it served as a military post, and after the war the barracks buildings became the Department of Education headquarters. The park was created in 1993 under an agreement between the City of Manila and a private environmental foundation (the Winner Foundation). Development pressure followed several times, such as plans for a school building or a gymnasium, but civic groups and environmental advocates opposed them and kept the park intact.

In February 2020, Manila City Ordinance No. 8607 declared it a permanent forest park, banning tree cutting, dumping of waste, excavation and illegal occupation. After redevelopment it reopened in February 2022, and it is now managed by the city, with security personnel reported to guard it in shifts around the clock. The relatively healthy secondary-growth forest holds dozens of tree species, including native trees such as amugis, narra, molave, balete and yakal. Reports differ on the number of trees, from about 1,500 to more than 3,000, so confirm the exact figure locally, but the dense shade of tall trees is unmistakable. The forest also cools the city, which makes it interesting for travelers who care about urban planning or the environment. Reports also say a plaza of about 5,100 square meters lies next to the park.

For travelers, the appeal here is coolness. During the El Niño heat wave in April 2024, city officials said ground temperatures inside the park were 3 to 4 degrees lower than elsewhere in the city. That makes it an excellent place to rest when you are tired from walking around Intramuros or the National Museum area. It is not an attraction with big rides or concession stands but a quiet place to walk, watch birds and sit, and you will enjoy it more if you go with that in mind. The park is within walking distance from the direction of the Manila Central Post Office and the Manila Metropolitan Theater, southeast of Intramuros, so it is easy to fit into an Ermita and Intramuros itinerary. There is also news that sections of the Pasig riverside promenade have been connected, so check current conditions before deciding to walk along the river from the post office to the park. A simple tip for first-timers: the forest is small and a slow loop takes about an hour, so do not spend a whole day on it, and treat it as a resting place between Ermita and Intramuros stops. Because this park was kept alive by the continuing efforts of citizens, the best manners are to stay on the paths, not harm trees or birds, and leave no trash. It is run by the City of Manila and operations may change, so check the latest announcements.

blocks.title: Shaded forest paths under tall trees

children.text: As you walk the tiled and concrete paths, large trees close in overhead. Native trees such as molave, narra, balete and sampaloc (tamarind) are mixed in, so it feels noticeably cooler even in the heat of midday. In places the trees have name tags or information boards, so stop and read them. You can see tropical species up close that are hard to find in Korea.
From the edge of the park you can look down on Quezon Bridge and the Pasig River. The contrast between the city across the water and the forest is a very Manila scene.

Birds such as the pied fantail, zebra dove, swallows and bulbuls have been reported, and some reports say more than 20 species use the park. During the migration season, an even wider variety of birds may be seen.
The park has a fountain, a fish pond and a small bridge, good for photos or sitting down to rest. It is small, but blends with the forest to feel like a garden.

blocks.title: The story of becoming a permanent forest park

children.text: Knowing that civic groups and teachers protected the park against development pressure gives your walk added meaning. Read the information boards near the entrance to learn about the trees and the park's history.

blocks.title: A site protected by teachers and citizens

children.text: In 2023 teachers held a protest event in the park, and in the same year a photo walk was held to protest restrictions on photography in public parks. These stories show how much the place matters to residents.

items.title: 1–2 hour forest walk
items.subtitle: A walk in the early morning or late afternoon

children.text: At the entrance on the Antonio Villegas Street side, follow any visitor sign-in procedure. Early hours are the coolest and quietest.
Walk slowly along the forest path and check the tree names on the information boards. This is a time of day with plenty of birdsong.
Rest on a bench by the fountain and pond. Take your trash with you.
Look at the Pasig River and Quezon Bridge from the riverside edge and take photos. Follow the on-site guidance on photography rules.
Leave by the exit and have lunch or a café break on the Ermita streets before moving on to your next stop.

items.title: Half-day Manila city route
items.subtitle: Linking the park with Ermita and Intramuros

children.text: Look around the exterior of the Manila Metropolitan Theater and the Central Post Office.
Rest in the shade at Arroceros Forest Park.
Head toward Intramuros and have lunch.
Explore Intramuros, including San Agustin Church and Fort Santiago.
Change the order of the route depending on the weather. On hot days, it helps to allow a longer rest at the park.
It is reported to be within walking distance of LRT-1 Central Terminal station.
The Lawton bus terminal and the Pasig River Ferry Lawton station are also fairly close. Check ferry operations locally.
Fares and schedules change often.
You can reach the park by taxi or ride-hailing from anywhere in Manila. Enter the destination as "Arroceros Forest Park, Antonio Villegas St., Ermita."
The road in front of the park is congested, so it may be easier to get off near Intramuros and walk.
Take a taxi or ride-hailing from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL); travel time varies greatly with traffic. Going via your hotel in Manila is the smoother plan.

Manila is comfortable for outdoor activities in the November–May dry season, though March–May is very hot. The forest here was reported to be cooler than the city at the same hour, so in hot months go in the morning or late afternoon.
The June–October rainy season brings showers and typhoon effects. Right after rain you can enjoy the birds and the scent of the trees, but paths can be slippery.

Of the day, right after opening is best. Sunlight filters through the leaves, there is plenty of birdsong, and it is easy to walk before the heat builds. Midday just after lunch is hot and humid even inside the forest, so avoid it. In the rainy season, visit in the morning, and if showers arrive in the afternoon, switch to indoor sights in Intramuros.

There is no lodging in the park itself, so it is easiest to stay in Ermita, Malate or around Intramuros. Ermita has many hotels and hostels within walking distance of the park. Compare hotel locations and rates in a booking app.
It is best to eat outside the park. Inside Intramuros and around Ermita there are many Filipino restaurants and cafés. Assume the park has almost no concession stands and bring water and snacks.

Ermita and Malate have Filipino home cooking, Korean restaurants and cafés clustered together, so it is easy to eat after your walk. Many Korean travelers decide on meals near their hotel, and water and light snacks are enough for the park.
Early morning and late afternoon are the coolest and have the most birds.
Opening and closing times differ by source, so check Manila city announcements or on-site notices just before you go.
Bring insect repellent, a hat and water. It is a forest, so there are mosquitoes.
Take your trash with you. Dumping is banned by ordinance and carries fines.
Follow the on-site photography rules, and check ahead for permission if you use professional equipment.
Fit it in as a resting stop between Intramuros and National Museum visits.
Do not touch or feed birds and animals.
Comfortable walking shoes are best. The paths are paved but can be wet after rain.
It is a fairly small park, so even a slow loop takes about an hour. Combine it with Intramuros or museum visits for a full-day plan.
With children, games such as finding tree names or listening for bird calls turn a short walk into a rewarding experience.
Opening hours and entry rules may change, so check the latest announcements before you visit.
This is downtown Manila, so watch for pickpockets and keep valuables out of sight.
The roads around the park are congested and some sidewalks are narrow.
Do not visit after dark.
Paths can be slippery in the rainy season.
Ordinance No. 8607 bans hunting, digging, dumping and unpermitted business.
Opening hours around the park may change, so leave before closing time.
A former theater in central Ermita, a good stop in the same district.
The Spanish-era walled city is close across the river and easy to add to the same day.
A museum district leading toward Rizal Park, reachable on foot.
Manila's best-known city park, good to visit together.
